nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a bounded open subset of a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $\gamma > 0$, $H$ any function of the gradient, and $f$ continuous on $\overline\Omega$. If $u$ is a viscosity subsolution and $v$ a viscosity supersolution of $\gamma u + H(Du) - f(x) = 0$ on $\Omega$, both continuous on $\overline\Omega$, and $u \le v$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $u \le v$ on $\Omega$.

nodes.summary: The Hamiltonian $F(x, r, p) = p(1)^2 - 1$ on $\mathbb{R}$, that is the equation $(u')^2 - 1 = 0$. Its classical solutions away from a point include both $|x|$ and $-|x|$; the viscosity notion selects one of them (see the eikonal example).
nodes.title: The one-dimensional eikonal Hamiltonian

nodes.summary: On a bounded open subset $\Omega$ of a finite-dimensional real inner product space, two viscosity solutions of $\gamma u + H(Du) = f(x)$ ($\gamma > 0$, $f$ continuous on $\overline\Omega$) that are continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and agree on $\partial\Omega$ agree on $\Omega$. Apply the comparison principle in both directions.
nodes.title: Uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem for $\gamma u + H(Du) = f(x)$

Then is a viscosity solution of $u_t + H(D_x u) = 0$ on $E \times (0, \infty)$, and $u(x', t) \to g(x)$ as $(x', t) \to (x, 0)$ with $t > 0$. Calder also states that it is the…
nodes.title: The Hopf–Lax formula

nodes.summary: On an open set $\Omega$, a $C^1$ function is a viscosity solution of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ if and only if $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0$ for every $x \in \Omega$. One direction is classical solutions are viscosity solutions; the other tests with $\varphi = u$ (subsolution, supersolution). So the viscosity notion extends, and does not change, the classical one.
nodes.title: Consistency of viscosity and classical solutions

nodes.summary: The function $u(x) = -|x|$ is a viscosity solution of $(u')^2 - 1 = 0$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$, kink included. Away from $0$ it is a classical solution. At $0$, every $C^1$ function touching $u$ from above satisfies $\varphi(t) - \varphi(0) \ge -|t|$ near $0$, so its slope lies in $[-1, 1]$ and $\varphi'(0)^2 - 1 \le 0$; and no $C^1$ function touches $u$ from below at $0$, so the supersolution condition is empty…
nodes.title: $-|x|$ is a viscosity solution of $(u')^2 - 1 = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be open. A function differentiable at every point of $\Omega$ with $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0$ there is a viscosity solution of $F = 0$ on $\Omega$: combine the subsolution and supersolution cases. Pointwise differentiability suffices; no continuity of $Du$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Classical solutions are viscosity solutions

nodes.summary: A viscosity solution of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ is a function that is both a viscosity subsolution and a viscosity supersolution on $\Omega$. Being upper and lower semicontinuous, it is continuous on $\Omega$. The name comes from the method of vanishing viscosity, which produces such solutions as limits of solutions of $F(x, u, Du) = \varepsilon \Delta u$; the theory itself makes no use of it…
nodes.title: Viscosity solution of a first-order equation

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be open. If $u$ is differentiable at every point of $\Omega$ and $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) \le 0$ for all $x \in \Omega$, then $u$ is a viscosity subsolution of $F = 0$ on $\Omega$.
nodes.title: Classical subsolutions are viscosity subsolutions

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a subset of a real normed space $E$ and $F : E \times \mathbb{R} \times E^* \to \mathbb{R}$. A function $u$ is a viscosity subsolution of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ if $u$ is upper semicontinuous on $\Omega$ and, whenever $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ function and $u - \varphi$ has a local maximum relative to $\Omega$ at $x \in \Omega$, The test function "touches $u$ from above" at $x$, and the inequality…
nodes.title: Viscosity subsolution of a first-order equation

nodes.summary: Let $\Omega$ be open. If $u$ is differentiable at every point of $\Omega$ and $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) \ge 0$ for all $x \in \Omega$, then $u$ is a viscosity supersolution of $F = 0$ on $\Omega$. The argument is that of the subsolution case, at a local minimum of $u - \varphi$.
nodes.title: Classical supersolutions are viscosity supersolutions

nodes.summary: A function $u$ is a viscosity supersolution of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ if $u$ is lower semicontinuous on $\Omega$ and, whenever $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ function and $u - \varphi$ has a local minimum relative to $\Omega$ at $x \in \Omega$, This is the mirror image of a viscosity subsolution, with test functions touching from below. The two notions are not exchanged by replacing $F$ with $-F$: see the eikonal…
nodes.title: Viscosity supersolution of a first-order equation

nodes.summary: The constant test function $0$ touches $|x|$ from below at $0$, and there $0^2 - 1 < 0$. So $|x|$ is not a viscosity supersolution, hence not a viscosity solution, of $(u')^2 - 1 = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$, although it solves the equation classically on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$. Compare $-|x|$, which is a viscosity solution.
nodes.title: $|x|$ is not a viscosity supersolution of $(u')^2 - 1 = 0$

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be jointly continuous and $\Omega$ open in a finite-dimensional real inner product space. If $u_n$ are continuous viscosity solutions of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ and $u_n \to U$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$, then $U$ is a viscosity solution on $\Omega$.
nodes.title: Stability of viscosity solutions under locally uniform limits

nodes.summary: If $u$ is $C^1$ and a viscosity subsolution of $F = 0$ on $\Omega$, then $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) \le 0$ at every $x \in \Omega$: take $\varphi = u$ itself as test function, since $u - u = 0$ has a local maximum everywhere. No openness of $\Omega$ is needed.
nodes.title: A $C^1$ viscosity subsolution is a classical subsolution

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be jointly continuous and $\Omega$ open in a finite-dimensional real inner product space. If $u_n$ are continuous viscosity subsolutions of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ and $u_n \to U$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$, then $U$ is a viscosity subsolution on $\Omega$.
nodes.title: Stability of viscosity subsolutions under locally uniform limits

nodes.summary: If $u$ is $C^1$ and a viscosity supersolution of $F = 0$ on $\Omega$, then $F(x, u(x), Du(x)) \ge 0$ at every $x \in \Omega$, by testing with $\varphi = u$.
nodes.title: A $C^1$ viscosity supersolution is a classical supersolution

nodes.summary: Let $F$ be jointly continuous and $\Omega$ open in a finite-dimensional real inner product space. If $u_n$ are continuous viscosity supersolutions of $F(x, u, Du) = 0$ on $\Omega$ and $u_n \to U$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$, then $U$ is a viscosity supersolution on $\Omega$.
nodes.title: Stability of viscosity supersolutions under locally uniform limits

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
